errors: Patch leaves the README typo 'recieve' in the sentence it rewrites (cosmetic).
Tests were run against a node:sqlite stand-in, not better-sqlite3 (disclosed).
V1-A.note: Complete patch covering both ship paths with a durable sent-at column, claim/unclaim retry, backfill of old shipped orders and tests it actually ran; only gap is no rollout or kill-switch step.

errors: By its own design a failed or lost e-mail is never resent, even on CSV re-upload (disclosed as a known gap and deferred).
Changes import semantics (skips bad lines, new response shape) beyond the request, though flagged.
V1-B.note: Sound status-transition design with full code and tests routed through one service function, but unrun, with no verification or rollout steps and the failure path only deferred.

errors: Failed sends are not retried (raised as question 2 with a follow-up); the first question, about which path is used, is low value.
V1-C.note: Minimal three-file diff that keeps markShipped synchronous, sends serially in the background, tests the bulk path, and adds concrete verification, rollout checks and a revert trigger; honest about being unrun.

errors: In-memory queue loses mail on restart and failures are dropped (disclosed); a malformed CSV line still throws mid-file (disclosed).
V1-D.note: Single shipOrder transition plus an in-process serial mail queue, an env kill switch, a quantified production gate and sharp prioritised questions; also spots the express.text body limit.

errors: Says the old parser crashed on CRLF; it does not (trim removes the carriage return), only blank or malformed lines crash.
Bulk import awaits every SMTP send inside the HTTP request (an explicit default, but the weakest choice for large CSVs).
A row with an empty tracking field would be marked shipped with an empty tracking code.
V1-E.note: Correct transition-based design with a transaction and tests, but keeps bulk sends inline in the request, defers failure handling to a follow-up and offers no rollout or verification beyond npm test.

errors: Stores the string 'pre-migration' in a timestamp column (minor).
Does not state that marketing_opt_in is ignored.
V1-F.note: Robust design (notified-at column, atomic claim, retry sweep, migration, transactional import) grounded in the repo, but mostly prose rather than code and two of its five questions are low value.

errors: The 30-day default grace period plus the purge sits right at the GDPR one-month limit it cites.
Purge deletes Postgres rows before the Stripe customer without saying where the Stripe id is kept.
V2-A.note: Best risk handling: blocks on shared workspaces, audits cascades, runs the purge in dry-run with go/no-go and abort rules, states the limit of rollback, and offers a cheaper manual path tied to what is driving the request.

errors: Never asks what drives the feature (legal requirement versus user requests).
V2-B.note: Compact and complete plan with good pitfalls (webhooks after deletion, workspace race, foreign-key audit) but no dry-run or go/no-go gate and no question about the driver.

errors: Defaults to no undo window, with the purge running within minutes, for an irreversible action; a grace period is only offered as an alternative.
Never asks what drives the feature.
V2-C.note: Tight, proportionate plan with inventory first and an idempotent purge, but its default is immediate irreversible deletion, and third parties and backups are only listed as out of scope.

errors: Step 2 hard-deletes sole-member workspaces at request time, which contradicts the 14-day restore; corrected only later in step 4.
Seven questions is more than needed.
V2-D.note: Very actionable ordered plan covering every trap, with edge-case tests, a dry-run rollout and a GDPR scope question; slightly heavy on questions and has one internal inconsistency.

errors: Deleting the Stripe customer in the purge sits awkwardly with keeping invoice records for tax.
Adds a whole ownership-and-billing-transfer phase based on an assumed billing model (scope growth).
V2-E.note: Strong safety design (database last, dry run, go/no-go, abort rule, OAuth grant revocation) but heavier than needed, and it only mentions GDPR timing rather than asking what drives the request.

errors: Says to roll back the database transaction if Stripe fails, but in its own ordering Stripe is called after that transaction.
Purge scrubs the user row before the Stripe customer step; seven questions is more than needed.
V2-F.note: Thorough phased plan covering every trap, with tests, a dry-run rollout and explicit v1 exclusions; small ordering sloppiness around Stripe.

errors: Defaults to the full switch 'as asked' despite arguing the cheaper path is right in most cases, so an unanswered question yields a multi-week migration.
V3-A.note: Most rigorous full-migration plan (AUTH_MODE flag, dual mode, revert rule, go/no-go, loss table) with the cheaper hybrid stated first, but long and defaulting to the questionable premise.

V3-B.note: Pushes back clearly, defaults to a hybrid (sessions for pages, JWT for the API), covers revocation, storage and keys, and gives a safe dual-read full-replacement path with rollback and effort estimates.

V3-C.note: Best premise challenge: maps each plausible driver to the right response, defaults to a hybrid, and still outlines a full replacement with dual-run migration, flag rollback and algorithm pinning.

errors: Its default plan builds JWT for a widget it assumes is same-origin, which by its own reasoning could keep using the session cookie; it then removes session auth from the API for no stated gain.
V3-D.note: Clear pushback and a small reversible plan (session-minted in-memory access token, no refresh token), but the default work is not justified under its own same-origin assumption.

errors: Defaults question 2 to 'must take effect at once', yet its design lets access tokens live up to 10 minutes after logout or a ban.
Rollback note ignores that logins after the switch to jwt mode create no sessions; defaults to the full switch.
V3-E.note: Thorough full-migration plan with flag, dual mode, revert rule and loss table, and the cheaper path stated up front, but heavy for a questionable premise and with small inconsistencies.

errors: No algorithm pinning; rollout and monitoring for the full path are only sketched.
V3-F.note: Concise and correct: challenges the premise, defaults to a hybrid, notes the same-origin widget needs no change, and outlines the full replacement with a dual period and a key-leak plan.
